scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4673: Hello, it's the IT department office here (our
machines are the 192.168.1.x ones). None of our computers can get to anything
on the network any more -- not the shared drives, not the other departments,
nothing, all of us at the same time. Someone here said "the department switch
has died" but honestly I wouldn't know which box that is or where it lives.
Could you check whatever connects our room to the rest of the campus and get
us back on? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The IT-segment switch is passing traffic: IT
  hosts (it_hod, it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach
  each other on 192.168.1.0/24. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of an L2 switch failure that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the IT-dept switch (switch0)
failed and took down the IT segment -- is NOT reproducible: IT hosts (it_hod,
it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach each other across
192.168.1.0/24, which means the L2 switch is passing traffic normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the IT-segment switch is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces IT host -> gateway and
host -> host pings, finds them all 0% loss (proving L2 connectivity through the
switch), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a failed switch -- declaring the
IT segment down to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Exhaustive diagnostic testing found no fault anywhere in the IT department's
network path or in the wider campus topology. All five IT machines
(it_hod/it_lab1–4, addresses 192.168.1.2–.6) have correct IP configuration
and a valid default route pointing to router0's eth0 (192.168.1.1). Switch0,
which bridges the IT LAN (lan_it, eth1) to the router0 uplink (link_r0_sw0,
eth0), is fully operational with both ports in UP/LOWER_UP state and the
bridge forwarding normally. Router0 runs FRR with RIP v2 correctly configured
on all three interfaces and holds a complete routing table: 192.168.1–2.0/24
directly connected, 192.168.3–4.0/24 learned via RIP from router1
(10.10.0.2), and 1.0.0.0/8 / 128.168.0.0/16 learned from router2. Router1
and router2 symmetrically hold return routes to 192.168.1.0/24 and
192.168.2.0/24, confirming full bidirectional reachability. Live ping tests
from multiple IT hosts to every other campus segment — office (192.168.3.2),
servers (1.0.0.5), CS (192.168.2.2), and principle (192.168.4.3) — all
returned 0% packet loss. No iptables ACL rules exist on any router. The
helpdesk complaint does not correspond to any actual network fault; the campus
network is operating correctly. No corrective action is required. The
submitter should be asked to re-test from their machines, as the issue may
have been transient or local to individual workstation configuration.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes IT hosts reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 and each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The writeup does not explicitly state IT hosts pinged the gateway 192.168.1.1 and each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss, only that they have correct routes and reached other segments.

The agent ran host route checks and multiple successful ping-pair tests to the gateway and across subnets, inspected router FRR status/config and iptables, and used that observed evidence to conclude no fault; switch interface output is partially truncated but end-to-end host connectivity substantiates L2 forwarding. Overall the claims are well-supported and the inferences follow logically with comprehensive coverage.
